blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 9 (Human Digestive System), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.
9.1 Anatomy and physiology of the digestive system

blocks.prompt: 1 Why is efficient digestion vital for sustaining life?
blocks.explanation: Digestion converts food into energy and raw materials for growth, repair and maintenance. It supports the immune system and provides essential nutrients; efficient digestion prevents nutrient deficiencies, supports metabolism and maintains energy levels.

book_ref.quote: Efficient digestion prevents nutrient deficiencies, supports metabolism and maintains energy levels

blocks.prompt: 2 Differentiate between the GI tract and the accessory digestive organs.
blocks.explanation: The human digestive system is made of these two components.

book_ref.quote: The human digestive system is composed of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and accessory digestive organs

rows: A continuous tube from mouth to anus
Organs outside the tube that help digestion
Oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small and large intestine
Salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas

blocks.prompt: 3 Give the structure and two functions of lips.
blocks.explanation: Lips are made of highly vascularized skeletal muscle tissue with many sensory nerve endings. They retain food while it is being chewed and play a role in phonation (modification of sound).

book_ref.quote: Lips help to retain food as it is being chewed

blocks.prompt: 4 How is food selected in the oral cavity?
blocks.explanation: The tongue tastes food through its taste buds and food is physically felt. If its taste or smell is unpleasant, or hard objects like bone or dirt are present, it is rejected. Smell and sight also help in selection.

book_ref.quote: If the taste or smell is unpleasant or if hard objects like bone or dirt are present in the food, it is rejected

blocks.prompt: 5 What is mastication? Why is it important?
blocks.explanation: Mastication (chewing) is the physical breakdown of ingested food by the teeth. It reduces food into smaller, manageable pieces and increases the surface area for enzyme action.

book_ref.quote: Chewing reduces food into smaller and more manageable pieces, increasing the surface area for enzymatic action

blocks.prompt: 6 Name the three pairs of salivary glands and give the location of each.
blocks.explanation: Sublingual glands: below the tongue. Submaxillary glands: behind the jaws. Parotid glands: in front of the ears.

book_ref.quote: submaxillary glands located behind jaws

blocks.prompt: 7 Differentiate between the roles of bicarbonate ions and thiocyanate ions of saliva.
blocks.explanation: Both are ions present in saliva along with water, mucus and salivary amylase.

book_ref.quote: Saliva also contains bicarbonate ions, which buffer chemicals in the oral cavity

rows: Buffer chemicals in the oral cavity
Kill microorganisms

blocks.prompt: 8 During swallowing, how is the entry of food into the nasal cavity prevented?
blocks.explanation: The tongue moves upwards and backwards against the roof of the mouth, forcing the bolus back, and the soft palate is raised against the back wall of the pharynx. These movements close the passage between the nasal cavity and pharynx.

book_ref.quote: These movements close the passage between nasal cavity and pharynx

blocks.prompt: 9 Is swallowing voluntary or involuntary? Explain.
blocks.explanation: Both. The beginning of swallowing, pushing the bolus to the back of the mouth, is voluntary; once the food reaches the back of the mouth, swallowing becomes automatic.

book_ref.quote: once the food reaches the back of the mouth, swallowing becomes automatic

blocks.prompt: 10 Give two functions of the cardiac sphincter.
blocks.explanation: The cardiac (lower oesophageal) sphincter controls the exit of food from the oesophagus to the stomach, opening in response to food pressure. It also prevents the backflow of stomach contents into the oesophagus.

book_ref.quote: which opens in response to the pressure exerted by food

blocks.prompt: 11 Differentiate between peristalsis and segmentation.
blocks.explanation: Both are movements of the alimentary canal.

book_ref.quote: Peristalsis squeezes the food down along oesophagus and other parts of the alimentary canal

rows: Rhythmic waves of contraction of smooth muscles in the walls
Rings of smooth muscle contract and relax repeatedly
Squeezes food along the oesophagus and other parts of the canal
Back-and-forth movement in the same place
Moves food forward
Mixes food with secretions; increases absorption efficiency
Throughout the alimentary canal
In small and large intestines

blocks.prompt: 12 Differentiate between antiperistalsis and hunger contractions.
blocks.explanation: Both are special forms of peristaltic movement.

book_ref.quote: creating the uncomfortable sensation known as hunger pangs

rows: Peristaltic movements reverse
Peristaltic movements triggered by low blood glucose
Push food from intestines back into stomach and oral cavity
Create the uncomfortable sensation of hunger pangs
Leads to vomiting
Lead to the feeling of hunger

blocks.prompt: 13 Name the three portions of the stomach and give the position of each.
blocks.explanation: Cardiac portion: immediately after the oesophagus. Fundus portion: on a side of the cardiac portion. Pyloric portion: beneath the cardiac portion.

book_ref.quote: The cardiac portion is present immediately after oesophagus

blocks.prompt: 14 Name the layers of the stomach wall, including its three muscle layers.
blocks.explanation: From outside: serosa; smooth muscle layer (outer longitudinal, middle circular and inner oblique muscles); submucosa; mucosa.

book_ref.quote: The outermost layer is serosa, the middle layer is made of smooth muscles

blocks.prompt: 15 What is pyrosis?
blocks.explanation: Pyrosis (heartburn) is a painful burning sensation in the chest caused by back flush of acidic chyme from the stomach into the oesophagus.

book_ref.quote: this condition is known as pyrosis or heartburn

blocks.prompt: 16 Name the three secretory cells of a gastric gland and the secretion of each.
blocks.explanation: Mucous cells: mucus, which protects the stomach lining from HCl and enzymes. Parietal (oxyntic) cells: hydrochloric acid. Chief cells: the enzyme pepsinogen.

book_ref.quote: Each gastric gland contains epithelial cells and three secretory cells

blocks.prompt: 17 Differentiate between pepsinogen and pepsin.
blocks.explanation: Pepsin is the active form of pepsinogen.

book_ref.quote: The H⁺ ions of the HCl activate pepsinogen into pepsin

rows: Secreted by chief cells
Formed in the stomach cavity from pepsinogen
Inactive form
Active enzyme; activated by H⁺ ions of HCl
Does not digest proteins
Breaks proteins into polypeptides and peptides

blocks.prompt: 18 What is the role of rennin in infants?
blocks.explanation: In infants the gastric juice contains large amounts of rennin. It coagulates milk proteins and delays the passage of milk into the small intestine; the delay lets other enzymes digest the milk proteins.

book_ref.quote: The delay enables other enzymes to digest the milk proteins

blocks.prompt: 19 How is the stomach mucosa protected from its own acid and pepsin?
blocks.explanation: Protection is provided in two ways: viscous mucus (secreted by mucous cells) covers the inside of the stomach, and bicarbonate neutralizes the acid.

book_ref.quote: The mucosa of stomach is susceptible to damage from acid and pepsin if it had no protection

blocks.prompt: 20 Differentiate between gastrin and somatostatin.
blocks.explanation: Both are hormones that regulate gastric secretion.

book_ref.quote: Gastrin is carried by blood to the gastric glands where it stimulates them to produce and secrete more gastric juice

rows: Released by endocrine cells of stomach mucosa when proteins are in food
Acts when food moves from stomach to small intestine
Stimulates gastric glands to secrete more gastric juice
Stops the release of hydrochloric acid

blocks.prompt: 21 Which two factors stimulate more gastric secretion once food arrives in the stomach?
blocks.explanation: The distension (stretching) of the stomach and the decrease in pH of the gastric contents stimulate more secretion and powerful contractions.

book_ref.quote: the distension of stomach and decrease in the pH of the gastric contents stimulate more secretion

blocks.prompt: 22 Name the parts of the small intestine with their lengths.
blocks.explanation: Duodenum: the first 20-25 cm. Jejunum: about 2.4 m, next to duodenum. Ileum: the last three-fifths, about 3.5 m. The whole small intestine is about 6 m long and 2-3 cm in diameter.

book_ref.quote: Small intestine consists of three parts i.e., duodenum, jejunum and ileum

blocks.prompt: 23 How is trypsin formed and what does it digest?
blocks.explanation: Pancreatic juice contains inactive trypsinogen. The enzyme enterokinase, secreted by the walls of the duodenum, activates it into trypsin, which digests proteins into polypeptides.

book_ref.quote: Trypsinogen, which is in inactive form

blocks.prompt: 24 Name four enzymes of pancreatic juice and the action of each.
blocks.explanation: Pancreatic amylase: polysaccharides into maltose (and even glucose). Trypsin: proteins into polypeptides. Pancreatic lipase: lipids into glycerol and fatty acids. Pancreatic nucleases: DNA and RNA into nucleotides. (Chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase: proteins into smaller peptides and amino acids.)

book_ref.quote: Pancreatic lipase, which digests lipids to glycerol and fatty acids

blocks.prompt: 25 Why cannot lipase readily attack fats without bile salts?
blocks.explanation: Fats are insoluble in water, so lipase cannot attack them readily. Bile salts act as detergent molecules that break fats into droplets and keep them separate, giving large surface areas for lipid-digesting enzymes.

book_ref.quote: So, they cannot be attacked readily by lipase enzymes of pancreatic juice

blocks.prompt: 26 Name four enzymes of intestinal juice and the product of each.
blocks.explanation: Aminopeptidase: polypeptides into dipeptides. Erepsin: dipeptides into amino acids. Maltase: maltose into glucose. Sucrase: sucrose into glucose and fructose. (Also lactase: lactose into glucose and galactose; lipase: fats into fatty acids and glycerol.)

book_ref.quote: The walls of jejunum and ileum contain glands which secrete intestinal juice

blocks.prompt: 27 Differentiate between chyme and chyle.
blocks.explanation: Both are forms of food mass in the alimentary canal.

book_ref.quote: the chyme is converted into an alkaline emulsion, called chyle

rows: Formed in the stomach, 3-4 hours after a meal
Formed in the small intestine after action of intestinal juice
Semi-liquid acidic mass
Alkaline emulsion

blocks.prompt: 28 Describe the structure of a villus.
blocks.explanation: A villus is a finger-like projection on the circular folds of jejunum and ileum. It is richly supplied with blood capillaries and a lymph vessel, the lacteal, both covered by a single-cell thick epithelium whose cells bear microvilli.

book_ref.quote: The total surface area of absorption becomes extraordinarily large due to villi and microvilli

blocks.prompt: 29 Differentiate between the absorption of glucose and of fatty acids.
blocks.explanation: Both are absorbed into the epithelial cells of villi in jejunum and ileum.

book_ref.quote: Simple sugars (e.g., glucose) and amino acids are absorbed by diffusion or active transport

rows: Absorbed by diffusion or active transport
Absorbed by passive transport
Enter blood capillaries of villi
Recombine into triglycerides, coated with protein as chylomicrons; enter lacteals
Carried by hepatic portal vein to the liver
Carried by thoracic lymphatic duct into the bloodstream

blocks.prompt: 30 What happens to chylomicrons after they enter the bloodstream?
blocks.explanation: Enzymes of blood plasma hydrolyse chylomicrons back into fats and proteins. The fats are ultimately hydrolysed into fatty acids and glycerol, which enter body cells.

book_ref.quote: Blood plasma has enzymes which hydrolyse chylomicrons back into fats and proteins

blocks.prompt: 31 What is the caecum? Why is the appendix called vestigial?
blocks.explanation: The caecum is a blind sac projecting from the large intestine between ileum and colon. From its blind end arises the finger-like vermiform appendix; in the human digestive system it performs no function, so it is vestigial.

book_ref.quote: It is a blind sac that projects from the area of large intestine between ileum and colon

blocks.prompt: 32 What is appendicitis? Why must an infected appendix be removed?
blocks.explanation: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, usually due to bacterial infection. It must be removed surgically (appendicectomy), otherwise it may burst and the inflammation may spread in the entire lining of the abdomen.

book_ref.quote: It is usually due to bacterial infection

blocks.prompt: 33 What are faeces composed of?
blocks.explanation: Faeces are wastes made more solid as the colon absorbs water. They consist of many bacteria, indigestible plant fibres (e.g. cellulose), other undigested food, sloughed-off mucosal cells, bile pigments and water.

book_ref.quote: These wastes products, called faeces, consist of a large number of bacteria

blocks.prompt: 34 Differentiate between the internal and external anal sphincters.
blocks.explanation: The anus, at the distal end of the rectum, is surrounded by these two sphincters.

book_ref.quote: Anus is surrounded by two sphincters

rows: Made of smooth muscles
Made of striated muscles
Relaxes automatically on rectal distension (reflex)
Consciously regulated in adults by the cerebral cortex

blocks.prompt: 35 What is the importance of bacteria living in the colon?
blocks.explanation: Bacteria like E. coli live and divide in the colon. During their metabolism they produce amino acids and vitamin K. Vitamin K, needed for blood coagulation, is absorbed from the large intestine into the blood.

book_ref.quote: Many bacteria, for example E. coli, live and actively divide within colon

blocks.prompt: 36 Differentiate between egestion in infants and in adults.
blocks.explanation: They represent two stages of neurological and muscular development.

book_ref.quote: In adults, egestion becomes voluntary as the cerebral cortex matures

rows: Involuntary reflex
Voluntary
Mediated by the spinal cord; higher brain centres not fully developed
Matured cerebral cortex controls it
Rectal distension relaxes the internal anal sphincter automatically
External anal sphincter consciously regulated to delay or start defecation

blocks.prompt: 37 Write four functions of the liver in digestion.
blocks.explanation: The liver produces bile, which emulsifies fats; it processes nutrients absorbed from the small intestine; it detoxifies harmful substances; it synthesizes proteins and stores glycogen for energy.

book_ref.quote: Bile emulsifies fats, making them easier to digest

blocks.prompt: 38 What is the role of the gallbladder? What are gall stones?
blocks.explanation: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile made by the liver and releases it through the bile duct when food enters the small intestine. Gall stones form when cholesterol secreted by the liver precipitates in the gallbladder; they may block the release of bile.

book_ref.quote: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver

blocks.prompt: 39 Differentiate between the exocrine and endocrine portions of the pancreas.
blocks.explanation: The pancreas is a large gland lying behind the stomach in the curve of the duodenum.

book_ref.quote: It has exocrine and endocrine portions

rows: Ducted
Ductless
Secretes pancreatic juice into the pancreatic duct, which enters the duodenum
Secretes insulin and glucagon into extracellular fluid, then into capillaries
Juice has enzymes for all food groups (trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipases, amylases, nucleases)
Hormones, not digestive enzymes

blocks.prompt: 40 Differentiate between secretin and cholecystokinin.
blocks.explanation: Both are hormones released by the duodenal walls that stimulate the pancreas to release pancreatic juice.

book_ref.quote: Similarly, the partially digested proteins and fats present in chyme stimulate the duodenal walls

rows: Released when the acidity of chyme stimulates the duodenal walls
Released when partially digested proteins and fats of chyme stimulate the duodenal walls
Stimulates the pancreas to release pancreatic juice
Stimulates the pancreas to release pancreatic juice and the gallbladder to release bile

blocks.prompt: 41 Write four metabolic roles of the liver.
blocks.explanation: It converts excess glucose into glycogen and back when needed; it breaks down fats for energy and forms cholesterol and lipoproteins; it converts amino acids and turns harmful ammonia into urea; it breaks down and removes toxins, drugs and alcohol from the blood (and regulates hormones).

book_ref.quote: It breaks down and removes toxins, drugs, and alcohol from the blood

blocks.prompt: 42 Name four kinds of nutrients stored in the liver.
blocks.explanation: Glucose (stored as glycogen); vitamins A, D, B₁₂ and K; minerals such as iron and copper; and fats and fat-soluble substances. They are released when the body needs energy or building materials.

book_ref.quote: It stores excess nutrients from the food and releases them when the body needs energy or building materials
